speaker: Albert Gu
title: No Priors Ep. 70 | With Cartesia Co-Founders Karan Goel & Albert Gu
question: In fundamental sequence-model research, how does working across different modalities like speech or vision actually shape core architecture design?
guest: I don't think multimodality by itself has been a driving motivation for this work, because I think of the models I've been working on as basic generic building blocks that can be used anywhere. They certainly can be used in multimodal systems to good effect. Different modalities have presented different challenges, which has influenced the design of these models, but I always look for the most general-purpose, fundamental building block that can be used everywhere. Multimodality is more of a different set of challenges in terms of how you apply the building blocks to that, but you still use the same techniques and they mostly work.

points.core: Core architecture research targets one general-purpose building block usable across every modality.
points.note: Accept: aiming for a single unified, modality-agnostic primitive/backbone rather than designing separate bespoke architectures for each modality. Do not credit: generic praise for multimodal AI without emphasizing a single general-purpose building block.

points.core: Different modalities act as stress tests exposing distinct failure modes in that primitive.
points.note: Accept: new modalities surface unique modeling challenges (e.g., long continuous streams, high sample rates) that feed back into refining the core architecture. Do not credit: claiming each modality requires custom domain-specific architectural layers.

points.core: Applying models multimodally becomes an application-layer challenge rather than a separate modeling paradigm.
points.note: Accept: once the fundamental building block is sound, the same core modeling techniques transfer across modalities with mostly application-level adaptation. Do not credit: claiming multimodality requires fundamentally different sequence-modeling mathematics.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly, modalities shape the edges of the model rather than its core, but they act as stress tests that expose which core assumptions are truly general.

The modern pattern is a largely modality-agnostic backbone (typically a Transformer) with modality-specific front ends: patch embeddings for images (ViT), convolutional downsampling or learned audio tokenizers for speech (wav2vec 2.0, Whisper), and subword tokens for text. The inductive biases that used to live in the architecture, such as convolutional locality for vision or recurrence for speech, have migrated into tokenization, positional encoding, and the training objective.

Where modalities do push on the core is through their statistics. Speech and video produce very long, highly redundant sequences, which drives work on efficient attention, hierarchical downsampling, latent bottlenecks (Perceiver), and state-space models like Mamba. Continuous signals lack a natural vocabulary, motivating vector quantization, masked prediction, and diffusion or contrastive objectives instead of plain next-token prediction. Vision's 2D structure prompted new positional schemes.

So a design that works across modalities is evidence it captures something fundamental rather than exploiting one domain's quirks.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Text masks fundamental sequence-modeling bottlenecks because fixed tokenizers pre-compress language into short, discrete, one-dimensional sequences with high semantic density. Moving to speech, raw audio, or vision strips away that crutch, exposing models to extreme sequence lengths, continuous high-frequency signals, low per-step information density, and multi-dimensional structure.

These pressures directly drive core architectural breakthroughs. Raw waveforms and high-resolution video break quadratic self-attention, motivating linear-time state-space models like S4 and Mamba alongside hybrid local-global mixers such as Conformers, where convolutions capture fine-grained local continuity before global routing occurs. Similarly, vision and audio force researchers to rethink rigid causal masking and one-dimensional indexing, yielding multi-dimensional rotary embeddings, resolution-agnostic continuous parameterizations, and hybrid blocks that blend causal autoregression with bidirectional or diffusion-style updates. Finally, because pixel patches and audio frames lack clean lexical boundaries, cross-modal work pushes sequence models toward learned, dynamic pooling—building adaptive hierarchical compression directly into the backbone rather than outsourcing representation granularity to static preprocessing.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Working across modalities mainly acts as a **stress test**. Each data type pushes on a different weakness, so a design that works on all of them is more likely to capture something general rather than one domain's quirks.

**Speech and raw audio** have very long, high-rate, continuous signals (about 16,000 samples per second). That rewards efficient long-range memory and smooth, time-invariant filters. This is why state-space models like S4 were first shown off on raw waveforms and long-range benchmarks.

**Language** is discrete and information-dense, so it needs content-dependent recall, such as copying specific tokens. Mamba's "selection" mechanism (input-dependent dynamics) came from exactly this gap. Its authors also reported a tradeoff: selection helped on text and DNA but could hurt on continuous audio, where the fixed, time-invariant behavior works better.

**Vision** adds 2D structure and no natural left-to-right order. That pushes researchers toward patching, bidirectional scans and mechanisms that don't depend on order.

Tokenization questions, like bytes versus learned chunks, also look different for each modality. That motivates models that learn their own segmentation.

The overall effect is that the core building block is shaped by the tensions between modalities, not by one benchmark. Many choices, such as discretization, gating and normalization, are compromises found by seeing where each modality breaks the model.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Working across modalities like speech and vision forces sequence-model researchers to confront structural properties that text alone obscures. Unlike discrete, information-dense text, audio and images are continuous, high-dimensional, and heavily redundant locally. Handling raw signals at practical sequence lengths drove architectural innovations in learned front-ends, such as patchification, convolutional downsampling, and hierarchical multi-scale representations that progressively compress resolution.

These longer, denser sequences also expose the quadratic bottleneck of standard self-attention, accelerating work on windowed or sparse attention, linear-time recurrences, and state-space models. Furthermore, because speech and vision rely heavily on local continuity and spatial or temporal geometry, they motivated hybrid blocks that pair local convolutions with global attention, alongside more expressive relative, rotary, and multi-dimensional positional encodings. Finally, contrasting modality demands—such as low-latency causal streaming in speech versus bidirectional spatial reasoning in vision—push researchers toward modular sequence-mixing backbones whose inductive biases, causality, and tokenization adapt cleanly across domains rather than remaining overfitted to text.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Working across modalities exposes assumptions that are easy to miss when designing for text alone. Speech arrives as densely sampled frames, so a model needs to capture short acoustic patterns, connect them across an utterance, and sometimes do both with limited lookahead. That makes choices such as temporal downsampling, local convolution, and causal attention part of the architecture. Vision makes a different assumption visible. Once an image is flattened into a sequence of patches, consecutive tokens don’t fully describe which patches are spatial neighbors. Two-dimensional position information and local attention can preserve that structure.

Comparing modalities helps researchers decide which mechanisms belong in a shared backbone and which depend on the input. Long-range information routing can be useful across text, speech, and vision, while tokenization, positional structure, and the amount of local context may need to differ. The comparison also tests whether an architectural gain reflects a broadly useful mechanism or an assumption that happens to fit one kind of data.

points.why: The response identifies mechanisms that could be shared but stops short of making a single modality-agnostic building block the goal of core architecture research.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Working across modalities changes what researchers ask an architecture to do. Text comes with discrete tokens in a natural order. Speech is continuous, and a single word can span many acoustic frames. If a model treats every frame as a token, attention spends much of its compute on nearly identical neighbors. That motivates designs that combine nearby frames before using attention to connect information across an utterance.

Vision exposes a different issue. Flattening an image into a sequence gives it an order, but two patches that touch in the image can end up far apart in that sequence. That motivates position representations that preserve two-dimensional relationships and attention patterns that combine local detail with broader context.

These experiments help researchers decide which responsibilities belong in the input representation and which belong in a shared sequence model. They can also yield ideas that travel back to text, such as processing long inputs at several levels of detail.
